The Fall River/New Bedford Line is a commuter rail line of the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) Commuter Rail system in southeastern Massachusetts, United States. It serves southeast Massachusetts by connecting Boston to Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford. The line is part of the South Coast Rail project and has undergone significant improvements.

Most of the line originated as the Fall River Railroad, which opened in segments between Fall River and South Braintree via Middleborough in 1845 and 1846. The railroad was built as part of the Old Colony Railroad, which connected Boston to New York City. Over the years, the line has undergone numerous changes, including the addition of branches to Fall River and New Bedford.

The Fall River/New Bedford Line runs south from Boston to Taunton, where it splits into branches to Fall River and New Bedford. It has 10 intermediate stations on the combined section. The line has been extended as part of the South Coast Rail project, which added five new stations to the line, extending west to Taunton.

The Fall River/New Bedford Line is operated by the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA). The line is part of the MBTA's Commuter Rail system, which connects various cities and towns in Massachusetts.

The Fall River/New Bedford Line has undergone significant improvements in recent years, including the extension of the line to Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford. The line plays a crucial role in connecting southeastern Massachusetts to the state capital, Boston. It also offers fare-free service from opening day until the end of March, providing a convenient and affordable transportation option for passengers.

![Image 1: Two trains pulled into the platforms at East Taunton Commuter Rail station](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2025-04/2025-03-24-south-coast-rail-east-taunton-opening.jpg?itok=BPrgcX6B)

The East Taunton station platform on the first day of Fall River/New Bedford Line service (March 24, 2025)

About This Project
------------------

![Image 2: Newly renovated New Bedford station with station sign and platform with yellow tactile surface indicator ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2024-06/2024-04-SCR-New-Bedford-Renovated-Station-Platform.jpg?itok=F511KnUe)

New Bedford station platform (April 2024)

The [South Coast Rail project](https://www.mass.gov/south-coast-rail) offers a reliable transit connection between southeastern Massachusetts and Boston. Riders can take a one-seat trip for the first time since the late 1950s.

The project creates connections between Boston and the communities of Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River, the only three major cities within 50 miles of Boston that previously didn’t have Commuter Rail access.

[Learn more about the South Coast Rail Program](https://www.mass.gov/service-details/about-the-south-coast-rail-project)

Building a Better T
-------------------

As part of our $9.6 billion, [5-year capital investment plan](https://www.mbta.com/cip), we're renovating stations, modernizing fare collection systems, upgrading services for our buses, subways, and ferries, and improving the accessibility of the entire system.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/projects)

Schedules
---------

On weekdays, trains run every 70 minutes. There are 32 direct trips to or from [South Station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-sstat) including:

*   15 trips between South Station and Fall River
*   17 trips between South Station and New Bedford

On weekends, there are 26 total trips with trains running every two hours.

[View the Fall River/New Bedford Line schedule](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable)

[Check alerts for the Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/alerts)

### Scheduled Transfers at East Taunton Station

In addition to the 32 direct trips to or from South Station on weekdays, we operate connecting trains between:

*   Fall River Depot and East Taunton station
*   New Bedford station and East Taunton station

Riders can transfer between connecting trains and direct trains at East Taunton station where the Fall River and New Bedford branches meet. This means riders on both branches can access more trips to or from South Station throughout the weekday.

For example, riders going between New Bedford and South Station can get to their destination even if the next direct trip is between Fall River and South Station:

1.   At New Bedford station, board the connecting train going to East Taunton station.
2.   At East Taunton station, exit the connecting train to make a transfer.
3.   Board the direct train that came from Fall River Depot and is continuing to South Station.

1.   At South Station, board the direct train going to Fall River Depot.
2.   At East Taunton station, exit the direct train to make a transfer.
3.   Board the connecting train going to New Bedford station.

We've coordinated train schedules to ensure that riders always have enough time to transfer at East Taunton.

* * *

Safety First Program
--------------------

**Safety First** is a program that educates people on how to stay safe around train tracks. Our goal is to bring an understanding of safety rules to all residents in every southeastern Massachusetts city and town.

Through presentations, brochures, videos, meetings, and conversations, you’ll learn safety basics.You can watch and share our [Safety Video Series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpgUaADAtNfuJKpPGysCprwkepiOC-DBZ) developed for children, teens, and the general public to learn about the importance of safety for everyone throughout the region.

Watch our safety videos, and please think **Safety First**.

To request rail safety education or materials, call Customer Support at [617-222-3200](tel:617-222-3200) or fill out our[Customer Support form](https://www.mbta.com/customer-support).

[Download a Safety First fact sheet](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2023-12-safety-first-fact-sheet.pdf)(PDF, 926 KB)

[### Commuter Rail Safety](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)
![Image 3: Bi-level Commuter Rail coaches at the newly-completed Freetown Station](https://live-mbta.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/styles/teaser/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-double-car-view.jpg?itok=9iFomq_d)

Commuter Rail safety is important to the MBTA. We aim to educate our riders and community members about Commuter Rail safety to prevent any accidents or close calls.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)

Construction Timeline
---------------------

South Coast Rail is being built in phases:

*   **Phase 1:** Extended the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line, now named the Fall River/New Bedford Line. Service on the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) started March 24, 2025.
*   **Full Build:** Extends the Stoughton Line south to connect more communities to the Fall River/New Bedford Line.

Phase 1 broke ground in July 2019, with major construction beginning in 2020. After we completed construction of stations, tracks, and signals, we also conducted rigorous testing to meet safety certifications and qualifications that precede passenger service.

Construction was divided into two contracts, with early action work preceding both:

*   Construction of the Fall River Secondary Line, which will connect Fall River to Boston
*   Construction of the New Bedford Main Line, the Middleborough Secondary Line, and the signal system for the entire Phase 1 corridor, which will connect Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River to Boston

[See a map of the Phase 1 corridor](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2024-12-18-south-coast-rail-phase-1-corridor-map-updated.pdf)(PDF, 9.1 MB)

![Image 4: A crew works on culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Culvert_Installation2020.jpg?itok=7KdZdwqv)

A crew replaces rail above a completed culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)

Our crews completed early action work in fall 2020 in preparation for Phase 1 construction:

*   Replaced four railroad bridges
*   Installed 46 culverts as part of the drainage system
*   Ordered and stored long-lead special track materials in advance to reduce construction delays
*   Constructed five wetland mitigation areas and began monitoring their success

[Learn more about early action work](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#spring-2019-fact-sheet-)

![Image 5: 16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service as part of the South Coast Rail project ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Bi-levelCoach.jpg?itok=-3Jgz3cU)

16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service during Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail project

In October 2019, the Fiscal and Management Control Board (FMCB) [approved the purchase of 16 bi-level coaches](https://www.mbta.com/news/2019-09-23/fmcb-approves-the-procurement-80-new-commuter-rail-bi-level-coaches) to meet the needs of the South Coast Rail project. The refurbishment of two locomotives required for South Coast Rail service is also complete. As of summer 2023, these vehicles are part of the state's commuter rail system inventory.

*   ![Image 6: Newly completed Freetown Station platform](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-platform-view.jpg?itok=rACkugcF)

The Completed Freetown Station during the ribbon-cutting event celebrating the substantial completion of the Fall River Secondary Line contract (December 2022) 
*   The Fall River Secondary Line extends to Fall River through Freetown and Taunton, providing direct service between Fall River and Boston.This new Commuter Rail line includes two stations in Freetown and Fall River, and a layover facility at Weaver’s Cove in Fall River. We completed construction at the end of 2024.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary Line, which was previously a freight line, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. Work also included tree clearing, erosion control, and survey work along the tracks. The tracks were reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included the following:

*   Nine rail bridges
*   10 new grade crossings and four interlockings
*   Two new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight

Trains on the completed Fall River Secondary Line travel through Berkley, Freetown, and Fall River.

[See a map of the Fall River Secondary Line](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FRS_Map.pdf)

![Image 7: view of rail layover yard with blue sky](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2025-01/2024-09-10-scr-wamsutta-layover-yard.jpeg?itok=BrdJ5T4o)

Wamsutta layover yard (September 2024)

The Middleborough Secondary Line extends from Middleborough through Taunton and into New Bedford to provide direct service between New Bedford and Boston.

The new Commuter Rail line includes four stations and a layover facility adjacent to the existing one in Wamsutta.

We completed construction for the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford Main lines in fall 2024. We completed construction for the pedestrian bridge at [New Bedford](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NBM-0546) station in spring 2025.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main lines, which are currently active freight lines, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. The right-of-way (ROW) was also reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included:

*   Six rail bridges, constructed to meet state-of-good-repair guidelines
*   18 grade crossings and 14 interlockings
*   Four new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight
*   Signal systems and [positive train control (PTC)](https://www.mbta.com/projects/commuter-rail-positive-train-control-ptc) for the entire Phase 1 corridor

Work took place in Middleborough, Taunton, Lakeville, Freetown, and New Bedford. Testing for the entire South Coast Rail occurred under this contract.

Work has been completed on the Fall River Secondary Line to overlay signals and communications.

[See a map of the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford lines](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_MSNBML_map.pdf)

[Read the press release](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-08-24/fmcb-approves-4035-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction)

The Full Build will extend Commuter Rail service on the Stoughton Main Line and Northeast Corridor (north of Canton Junction). It will bring service to Taunton and connect more communities in the region.

This stage presents more challenges related to wetland impacts, complex engineering, electrification, and cost. The next steps include starting conceptual design work, preliminary engineering, and securing funding.

[See a map of the Full Build corridor](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FullBuild_CorridorMap_2020.pdf) (PDF, 793 KB)

Fall River / New Bedford Line
=============================

Enjoy the Coastal Charm of Southeastern Massachusetts
-----------------------------------------------------

Convenience with the Commuter Rail
----------------------------------

(Service now extended from Middleborough to 6 new stations!)
------------------------------------------------------------

Head into Boston or get away from the hustle and bustle of the big city and discover the South Coast with a little help from the Commuter Rail. The Fall River/New Bedford Line offers a convenient way to get to Boston while avoiding the highway traffic on Route 24 and the Southeast Expressway. If you live near Boston, getting to Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard just got a little more car-free! Just take the Fall River/New Bedford Line to [New Bedford Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/new-bedford/) and catch the free weekend shuttle from the Whale’s Tooth parking lot (near the New Bedford Station) to the [New Bedford Ferry Terminal](https://www.newbedfordferries.com/). Check[ferry schedules](https://seastreak.com/what-to-know/port-locations-directions-parking/new-bedford-ma/) prior to your trip.

The Fall River/New Bedford Line runs from Boston’s [South Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/south-station/) through Middleborough and East Taunton to one of two branches: one continuing to [Fall River](https://massbytrain.com/stations/fall-river-depot/) and the other to [New Bedford](https://massbytrain.com/stations/new-bedford/). Additional shuttle trains operate between East Taunton and the two branches, offering train connections between Boston and both the Fall River and New Bedford branches on most trips.

With the $10 Weekend Pass, ride the Commuter Rail as often as you’d like during weekends and holidays, and explore cultural gems along the line like the [New Bedford Whaling Museum](https://www.whalingmuseum.org/), [Lizzie Borden House](https://lizzie-borden.com/), [Battleship Cove](https://www.battleshipcove.org/), [Adams National Historical Park](https://www.nps.gov/adam/index.htm), or the [JFK Library](https://www.jfklibrary.org/). Whether you are taking the train for work, or special events like sports games or concerts, the Fall River/New Bedford Line will get you there with ease.

[Learn More](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/#itineraries-and-stories)[Buy Tickets](https://www.mbta.com/fares/commuter-rail-fares)

The **Fall River/New Bedford Line** (formerly the **Middleborough/Lakeville Line**) is a [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") line of the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system in southeastern [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), United States. It runs south from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"), where it splits into branches to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts") and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). There are 10 intermediate stations on the combined section and one on each branch. With a distance of 60 miles (97 km) from Boston to New Bedford and 56.6 miles (91.1 km) to Fall River, it is the second-longest line in the system.

Most of the line originated as the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_(1846) "Fall River Railroad (1846)"), which opened in segments between Fall River and [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_(MBTA) "Braintree station (MBTA)") via Middleborough in 1845 and 1846. At South Braintree, it met the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_(1844%E2%80%931854) "Old Colony Railroad"), which provided a connection to Boston. The two railroads merged in 1854 to form the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). While the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") largely replaced the line as a Boston–Fall River route in 1866, it remained busy with commuter and Boston–[Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") traffic. Mergers brought it under the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") in 1872 and the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893.

Commuter service peaked in the early 20th century and began to decline in the 1910s. Service on the Fall River–Middleborough segment ended in 1931. After two decades of attempts to end Old Colony Division service, the New Haven terminated it in 1959. Planning for the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") to restore service on the Middleborough line began in the 1970s. Construction began in 1993, and service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line began in 1997. Seasonal [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") excursion service began using the line in 2013. The line was extended and renamed in 2025 as part of the first phase of the [South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") project. An extension from Middleborough to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") or [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") is proposed.

[![Image 3: A passenger train at a high-level platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Photo_op_train_at_Freetown_station%2C_December_2022.jpg/250px-Photo_op_train_at_Freetown_station%2C_December_2022.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photo_op_train_at_Freetown_station,_December_2022.jpg)

Freetown station prior to opening

The northern portion of the line follows the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line"), which runs approximately north–south from Boston to Middleborough. The northernmost section from [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station") through Boston, [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts"), and [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree,_Massachusetts "Braintree, Massachusetts") is shared with the [Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line "Kingston Line") and [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 47  The line continues south through [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Massachusetts "Randolph, Massachusetts"), [Holbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holbrook,_Massachusetts "Holbrook, Massachusetts"), [Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon,_Massachusetts "Avon, Massachusetts"), [Brockton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockton,_Massachusetts "Brockton, Massachusetts"), [West Bridgewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bridgewater,_Massachusetts "West Bridgewater, Massachusetts"), [East Bridgewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bridgewater,_Massachusetts "East Bridgewater, Massachusetts"), and [Bridgewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgewater,_Massachusetts "Bridgewater, Massachusetts"). Intermediate stations are served at [JFK/UMass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station "JFK/UMass station"), [Quincy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station"), [Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_(MBTA) "Braintree station (MBTA)"), [Holbrook/​Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holbrook/Randolph_station "Holbrook/Randolph station"), [Montello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montello_station "Montello station"), [Brockton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockton_station_(MBTA) "Brockton station (MBTA)"), [Campello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campello_station "Campello station"), and [Bridgewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgewater_station_(MBTA) "Bridgewater station (MBTA)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 3

In downtown Middleborough, it turns west at Pilgrim Junction just north of [Middleborough station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station"). It follows the [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary") west to Cotley Junction in southern [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"), then the [New Bedford Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Main_Line "New Bedford Main Line") southeast to [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") via [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station"). From Myricks, the New Bedford Branch follows the New Bedford Main Line to [New Bedford station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_station "New Bedford station") via [Church Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Street_station_(MBTA) "Church Street station (MBTA)"), while the Fall River Branch follows the [Fall River Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Secondary "Fall River Secondary") to [Fall River station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_station "Fall River station") via [Freetown station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown_station "Freetown station").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 48

Like the rest of the MBTA Commuter Rail system, the line operates using [push-pull trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Push-pull_train "Push-pull train") with diesel locomotives. Maximum speeds are 79 miles per hour (127 km/h) south of Braintree and 59 miles per hour (95 km/h) to the north.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 12 [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 53  The line is mostly single track with passing sidings; there is some double track in Boston, Quincy, Braintree, and Brockton, and between Cotley Junction and Myricks Junction.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 11 [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 52  Layover yards for the line are located in Fall River and New Bedford, plus an older yard in Middleborough.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 7, 47  All stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 10 [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 56–58

As of October 2025, the portion between East Taunton and Boston has 16 round trips on weekdays and 13 on weekends. These trips are split approximately equally between the Fall River and New Bedford branches. On weekdays, most Boston trains have a shuttle train serving the other branch, with a [cross-platform transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-platform_transfer "Cross-platform transfer") at East Taunton. Typical running times for through trains are 94 to 109 minutes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-4) The [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") operates one daily round trip between Boston and Hyannis on Friday evenings, Saturdays, and Sundays during the summer tourist season (typically [Memorial Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Day "Memorial Day") weekend in late May to [Labor Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day") weekend in early September). It uses the portion of the line north of Middleborough with stops at Braintree and Brockton.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)

#### Old Colony Railroad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Old Colony Railroad")]

[![Image 4: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/OC1893.jpg/250px-OC1893.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OC1893.jpg)

Map of the Old Colony Railroad in 1893

The [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_(1846) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") was formed in March 1845[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-8) as the merger of three smaller railroads. It opened in phases from June 9, 1845 to December 21, 1846, forming a line between Fall River and South Braintree via Middleborough.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1911report-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-10) At South Braintree, it connected with the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_(1844%E2%80%931854) "Old Colony Railroad"), which had opened between Boston and [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth,_Massachusetts "Plymouth, Massachusetts") on November 10, 1845.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95  In 1847, the railroad opened a short extension to [Fall River Wharf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship_Cove_station#History "Battleship Cove station") and began [Fall River Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Line "Fall River Line") rail–steamboat service between Boston and New York.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 403  The [Cape Cod Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad") opened from Middleborough to [Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwich,_Massachusetts "Sandwich, Massachusetts") on [Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") in 1848 and to [Hyannis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyannis,_Massachusetts "Hyannis, Massachusetts") in 1854.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 411  The Old Colony and the Fall River merged in 1854 to form the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). Schedules permitted commuting to Boston from as far south as Bridgewater from then onwards. [North Bridgewater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockton_station_(MBTA)#History "Brockton station (MBTA)") (later renamed Brockton) was a turnback point for [short turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_turn "Short turn") trains in the late 1850s and early 1860s.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95

The [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad"), owned by the Old Colony and Newport (1863 successor to the Old Colony and Fall River), opened in September 1866. It connected to the Fall River Railroad line at Braintree Highlands and Somerset Junction, providing a shorter Boston–Fall River route that also served [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"). The Dighton and Somerset became the railroad's primary Boston–Fall River route, but the older route remained busy with Cape Cod traffic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 393, 403  The Old Colony and Newport Railroad and the Cape Cod Railroad merged in 1872 to form the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad"). [Campello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campello_station "Campello station") in southern Brockton was a turnback point from the early 1870s on.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95

Continued traffic growth led the Old Colony to [double-track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_track_railway "Double track railway") several of their main lines in the 1880s and 1890s.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95 [[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-12) Double track was extended south from South Braintree to Randolph in 1882, to Campello in 1883, to Bridgewater in 1884, and Middleborough in 1885.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-13) Schedules were consistently suitable for commuting from Middleborough after the mid-1880s.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95  The [West Bridgewater Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=West_Bridgewater_Branch&action=edit&redlink=1 "West Bridgewater Branch (page does not exist)"), which connected the line with the Dighton and Somerset, was completed in 1888.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 405  Double track was completed from Middleborough to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") in 1893.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-14) Schedules permitted commuting from Cape Cod beginning in 1894.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95

[![Image 5: A postcard showing two stone railway stations flanking elevated tracks in a city](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Brockton_station_white_border_postcard.JPG/250px-Brockton_station_white_border_postcard.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brockton_station_white_border_postcard.JPG)

Postcard of the 1890s-built Brockton station

The [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") leased the Old Colony in 1893.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 393  A construction project lasting from 1894 to 1897 elevated the tracks through downtown Brockton to eliminate grade crossings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-snow-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-elevation-16) Service on the Middleborough line was at its peak from about 1898 to 1914. In 1898, daily inbound service to Boston included six trains from Cape Cod, three from Fall River, six from Middleborough, seven from Campello, and one from [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station") via the [West Bridgewater Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=West_Bridgewater_Branch&action=edit&redlink=1 "West Bridgewater Branch (page does not exist)"). There were also three trains from [Montello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montello_station "Montello station") to Boston that operated south from Montello through Brockton then used branchlines to reach Boston.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 34, 96 [[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-17) Numerous trains from the Old Colony Division's many branches used the mainline north of Braintree; many of them split and merged at Braintree.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96

The middle section of the original Fall River Railroad, between Middleborough and [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts"), lost importance after the turn of the century, though commuter service from Fall River was available for several years beginning in 1915.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95 [[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 403  Service levels began to decline during World War I when freight was given priority and continued to decline thereafter. Commuter-suitable service was not always available from Cape Cod after 1919.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95–96  By 1924, inbound service included five trains from Cape Cod, one from Fall River, five from Middleborough, three from Bridgewater, eight from Campello, and one from [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton_station "North Easton station") via the West Bridgewater Branch (on which service ended in 1925).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-18)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96  Fall River service via Middleborough ended in 1931.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96

A train at Middleborough around 1940

The New Haven Railroad declared bankruptcy in 1935, setting off a [12-year-long reorganization process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad#Financial_difficulties_(1935%E2%80%931969) "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad"). The Old Colony lease was a major liability to the New Haven. It ended the lease in 1936 but was forced to continue operating the division.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-interest-19): 499 [[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 12  In the [88 stations case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88_stations_case "88 stations case"), the New Haven controversially closed 88 stations in Massachusetts on July 17, 1938.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 13 [[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-timetables-21) Three were on the Middleborough line and three more between Middleborough and the [Cape Cod Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Canal "Cape Cod Canal").[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-23) In May 1939, the company proposed to abandon all passenger service in the "Boston Group" – the primary group of lines into Boston, including the [Greenbush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line#History "Greenbush Line"), [Plymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston_Line#History "Kingston Line"), and Middleborough lines and the shared mainline north of Braintree.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-interest-19): 501 [[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 15  A revised proposal that September was to keep Boston–Braintree service plus limited commute-hour service as far as Campello, [Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitman_station "Whitman station"), and Hingham.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-24)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 16

After further controversy, a compromise schedule took effect on March 31, 1940, with service cut nearly in half but no lines abandoned.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-25)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 21  This schedule only required use of a single track and passing sidings south of Bridgewater; the second track between Bridgewater and Buzzards Bay was removed over the following two years.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 22  On February 18, 1941, the [Interstate Commerce Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Commerce_Commission "Interstate Commerce Commission") refused abandonment of the Boston Group, forcing the New Haven to continue operations on the Old Colony.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1942report-26) Additional traffic during World War II temporarily boosted the railroad's fortunes, but the postwar years again saw mounting deficits on the Old Colony Division. Sharp cuts in March 1949 removed most off-peak service; the Middleborough line was left with two inbound trains from Cape Cod and three from Middleborough.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 13, 96 [[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem2-27): 17

Under the 1951–1954 presidency of [Frederic C. Dumaine Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_C._Dumaine_Jr. "Frederic C. Dumaine Jr."), the New Haven increased passenger service, using new [Budd Rail Diesel Cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Rail_Diesel_Car "Budd Rail Diesel Car") to reduce costs.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 13 [[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 10  By April 1954, there were three daily inbound trains from Cape Cod, four from Middleborough, and six from Brockton.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96  However, Patrick B. McGinnis taking the railroad's presidency in 1954 resulted in deferred maintenance and cancelled plans for further service expansion.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 12  The New Haven again proposed to abandon all Old Colony service. A temporary state subsidy was introduced in 1958 to continue Greenbush, Plymouth, Middleborough, and Cape Cod service for an additional year while the [Southeast Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Expressway_(Massachusetts) "Southeast Expressway (Massachusetts)") and other highways were under construction.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 23  The final day of service was June 30, 1959, as the subsidy expired. Bus companies including the [Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Massachusetts_Street_Railway "Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway") and [Plymouth and Brockton Street Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_and_Brockton_Street_Railway "Plymouth and Brockton Street Railway") expanded their South Shore commuter service.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26

The Red Line in Quincy in 1973

In early 1960, state and Cape Cod officials reached an agreement with the New Haven to operate Boston–Cape Cod and New York–Cape Cod service during the busy summer tourist season.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26  The New York trains, the [_Day Cape Codder_ and _Neptune_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Codder_(NH_train) "Cape Codder (NH train)"), operated as planned.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-lynch-30) However, the wooden trestles of the drawbridge carrying the Old Colony main line over the [Neponset River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neponset_River "Neponset River") between Boston and Quincy burned on the night of July 22–23, 1960.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-31) The New Haven collected insurance money but refused to rebuild the bridge, instead rerouting freight trains via Middleborough.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26 [[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 19  For passengers, connections were provided between [Shore Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") trains and New York–Cape Cod trains at [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro_station_(Massachusetts) "Attleboro station (Massachusetts)"). For the 1961 season, Boston–Cape Cod service ran via Stoughton.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26  The New York trains ran until 1964.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-lynch-30) Freight service continued to use the Middleborough line.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 404

The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in August 1964 as an expansion of the urban Metropolitan Transit Authority into the surrounding suburbs. The MBTA was intended to subsidize commuter rail service – and to replace much of it with rapid transit extensions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 13  The MBTA's first such project was a branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(MBTA) "Red Line (MBTA)") (Cambridge–Dorchester Line) following the Old Colony alignment to Braintree.[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-35) In November 1965, the MBTA purchased the Old Colony main line between Boston and South Braintree from the New Haven.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-36)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 22  By 1966, the MBTA expected to eventually extend the line to Braintree Highlands or Holbrook on the Middleborough line, with a spur to [Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Massachusetts "Weymouth, Massachusetts") or [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 24  The Red Line opened to [Quincy Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") in September 1971 and [Braintree station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_(MBTA) "Braintree station (MBTA)") in South Braintree in March 1980.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36  Within Boston, a single freight track paralleled the new tracks. Although there was no freight service through Quincy, a single-track right-of-way was reserved for future freight use when the extension was built.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): i, 1, 4

The New Haven Railroad merged into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central") at the end of 1968.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 15  In 1970, following [revolts against freeways in the urban core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_revolts_in_the_United_States#Massachusetts "Highway revolts in the United States"), Massachusetts governor [Francis Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Sargent "Francis Sargent") placed a moratorium on new highway construction inside the [Route 128 beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_(Massachusetts)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded Southeast Expressway would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 16  In January 1973, the MBTA acquired most of Penn Central's suburban lines around Boston, including the Middleborough line as far south as Campello.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-37)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-38)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-39)

[![Image 8: A passenger train crossing a high girder bridge over a river](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg/250px-MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg)

A major part of the Old Colony Lines restoration was the George L. Anderson Bridge over the Neponset River.

A 1974 state report evaluated potential service as far as Hyannis and Falmouth on Cape Cod. It estimated construction costs of $13.6 million to $23 million (equivalent to $67–113 million in 2024), plus $9.2 million ($45 million) for purchasing the tracks and $2.5 to $6.8 million ($12–34 million) for equipment.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-40) On October 15, 1979, a special train ran from Braintree to Middleborough to publicize the state's plans for restored service.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-secondsection-41) In 1984, a state-directed MBTA study found that restoration of commuter rail service on the former Old Colony lines would be feasible.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4  During the summers of 1984 to 1988, the [Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_and_Hyannis_Railroad "Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad") operated passenger service between Braintree station and Cape Cod. Intended partially as a precursor to full commuter rail service, it made five intermediate stops (Holbrook, Brockton, Bridgewater, Middleborough, and Wareham) between Braintree and Buzzards Bay.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-43)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-anew-44)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-45)

A Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for restoration of service on the Middleborough, Plymouth, and Greenbush lines was released in May 1990.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-46) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1991agreement-47)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-48)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-49) The Final Environmental Impact Statement for the Middleborough and Plymouth lines – often called the "Old Colony Lines" – was released in 1992.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-50)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-51) Two station sites considered in the DEIS – Westdale in West Bridgewater and Middleborough/[Route 44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_44 "Massachusetts Route 44") in northern Middleborough – were dropped from consideration.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4

Construction of the $560 million project began in 1993, with service then expected to begin in late 1996.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-52) Which stations to include on the shared mainline between Braintree and Boston proved controversial. Original plans called only for a stop at Braintree.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 8  In September 1995, state governor [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Weld "Bill Weld") announced that a platform would be built at [Quincy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") instead.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-53) Later that year, the MBTA agreed to build both stations.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-54) In November 1996, the MBTA agreed to add a stop at [JFK/UMass station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station "JFK/UMass station") as well.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55) Limited weekday service with four daily round trips each on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line and [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line") began on September 29, 1997.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-56)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-57) Full service began on November 30, 1997. The Middleborough/Lakeville Line had twelve round trips on weekdays and seven on weekends.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-58)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-59) Weekend and some weekday trains began stopping at JFK/UMass on April 30, 2001.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55)

In 2007, [concrete ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_sleeper "Concrete sleeper") used on the Old Colony Lines began to fail due to manufacturing errors. The rate of failures increased during the following two winters, affecting service and causing speed restrictions.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-60) In 2010, the MBTA began a project to replace the 150,000 failing ties, which were part of a batch of 600,000 made in the 1990s, with wooden ties.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-62) Some replacement work in Bridgewater and Middleborough took place in 2010.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-beacon-ties-61) Midday service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line was replaced by buses from March 14 to June 6, 2011.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-64) Weekend service on the line was replaced from March 26 to December 18, 2011, and March 17 to April 22, 2012.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-65)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63) The project was completed in May 2012 at a cost of $91.5 million.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-66)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-67)

On May 24, 2013, the MBTA began operating [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") service between Boston and Hyannis over the Middleborough Main Line and Cape Main Line. Service consisted of one daily round trip on Friday evenings, Saturdays, and Sundays during the summer tourist season.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-70) In 2013 and 2014, the Friday evening southbound train operated as an extension of a regular Middleborough/Lakeville Line train, while Saturday and Sunday service operated with a separate trainset. In 2015, Friday CapeFlyer service also began using a separate trainset.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-71)

Substantially reduced schedules were in effect on the Commuter Rail system from March 16 to June 23, 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5) Schedule changes effective November 2, 2020, added midday service with consistent 60-to-70-minute midday headways on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line, though a pilot of late-night service was discontinued.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-72) Temporary reduced schedules were again put into place from December 14, 2020, to April 5, 2021.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-73)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-74) By October 2022, Middleborough/Lakeville service was at 77% of pre-COVID ridership.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-oct2022ridership-1)

Middleborough station near completion in August 2023

In the 1980s — during the first expansion of commuter rail service in Massachusetts in decades — the restoration of service to New Bedford and Fall River ([South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail")) was proposed. Three routes were considered, including the Middleborough Main Line and Middleborough Secondary. By 1988, the MBTA was tentatively planning to use a route via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-75) A 1995 feasibility study found that the limited capacity of the single track between Boston and Braintree could only support service to Fall River or New Bedford, but not both.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1995report-76) Planning for the Stoughton route continued until it was suspended in 2003.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-srpedd-77) Planning restarted several years later. The 2009 alternatives analysis report, 2011 draft [environmental impact statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_statement "Environmental impact statement"), and 2013 final environmental impact statement all chose the Stoughton route.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-78)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-DEIS-79)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FEIS-80)

In June 2016, the MBTA announced that the project cost had been revised to $3.42 billion, with completion not expected until 2030. The substantial delay and increase in cost caused officials to consider alternate plans, including an interim service to New Bedford via Middleborough. Some local and regional officials objected to that plan, as it would have reduced service to Middleborough/Lakeville station and potentially interfered with Plymouth/Kingston Line and Greenbush Line service.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june2016-81)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-82) In March 2017, the state announced a revised plan intended to provide service sooner for a total cost of $3.42 billion. The $1.1 billion Phase 1 would follow the Middleborough route and open in 2024 with service to both Fall River and New Bedford. Phase 2 would follow the Stoughton route (including electrification) and open in 2029.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-gears-83) Middleborough and Lakeville officials were critical of the possibility of abandoning Middleborough/Lakeville station— which had attracted [transit-oriented development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit-oriented_development "Transit-oriented development")— or requiring its riders to take a shuttle train.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sharp-84)

By June 2017, the Phase 1 completion date was moved to 2022.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-85) The draft supplemental environmental impact report was issued in January 2018. It analyzed three options for Middleborough: a reverse move to serve the existing station, a new Middleborough station with a rail shuttle between the existing station and Bridgewater, and a new Middleborough station with a bus shuttle from the developments at the existing station site. The third option was chosen for higher operational flexibility, lower travel times, and avoiding the need to add double track between Middleborough and Bridgewater.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 19

The two main construction contracts for the project were awarded in May and August 2020. By then, service was expected to begin in late 2023.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FRaward-86)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-87) Overall project completion reached the halfway point in mid-2022.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-88) In September 2023, the MBTA indicated that revenue service would not begin until mid-2024.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-89) In April 2024, the MBTA acknowledged that a midyear opening was unlikely but did not provide a new schedule.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-90)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-91) In June 2024, the MBTA announced that the planned opening had been delayed again to May 2025.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-92)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-93) Service began on March 24, 2025. The line was renamed as the Fall River/New Bedford Line at that time.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-march24-94)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-95) Weekday service on the main portion of the line increased from 14 round trips to 16; weekend service increased from 10 round trips to 13.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-scr-schedule-96)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-97)

The months after the extension saw several service quality issues.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) A shortage of rail crews caused some trains to be cancelled during the first several weekends.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-99) The MBTA preemptively replaced some trips with buses on the weekends of April 19–20 and 26–27.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-100)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-101)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-102) One third of trains were late during the first two weeks of extended service, versus one-tenth systemwide. On-time performance improved thereafter but remained below the rest of the system through April and May. The MBTA blamed "startup conditions" and difficulty coordinating trains on the mostly-single-track line for the issues.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) On July 21, 2025, the schedule was changed to improve reliability. This included removal of off-peak and weekend stops at JFK/UMass, removal of two late-night shuttle trains, and longer running times.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-103)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-104) By November 2025, daily ridership on the line was about 2,000 higher than a year before.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-105)

### Cape Cod service proposals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Cape Cod service proposals")]

[![Image 11: A Spanish revival style railway station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg/250px-Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg)

[Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station"), a possible future terminus of service

In 2007, the Boston Region Metropolitan Planning Organization released a feasibility study of extending commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay,_Massachusetts "Buzzards Bay, Massachusetts"), a portion of [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne,_Massachusetts "Bourne, Massachusetts") on the north side of the [Cape Cod Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Canal "Cape Cod Canal"). Intermediate stops were to be at Rock Village in southern Middleborough, County Road on the [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Massachusetts "Rochester, Massachusetts")/[Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham,_Massachusetts "Wareham, Massachusetts") border, and [downtown Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham_Village_station "Wareham Village station").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2007study-106) The introduction of the CapeFLYER brought new attention to the possibility of extending the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to Buzzards Bay.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-possibility-107) Later in 2013, the Wareham Chamber of Commerce and Buzzards Bay town selectmen both indicated support for Buzzards Bay commuter rail based on the success of the CapeFLYER, the Chamber supported the extension of commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-108)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-109)

[MassDOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MassDOT "MassDOT") and the Cape Cod Commission both studied the potential service in 2014–15. The studies estimated daily ridership of 800 to 875 if all Middleborough/Lakeville trains were extended to Buzzards Bay without intermediate stops.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2015study-110) Bourne voted to join the MBTA district in 2015 and began paying an [assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_assessment "Tax assessment") in mid-2016, although there was no guarantee that commuter rail service would be provided.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-111) MassDOT began planning a possible trial service in October 2015. The service was to have shuttle trains between Bourne and Middleborough/Lakeville operated by [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-rausch-112) The MBTA Fiscal Management and Control Board rejected the service proposal in April 2016.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-113)

During the South Coast Rail project, Middleborough station was designed with space for a shuttle platform to be added later.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 38  In 2021, MassDOT released a feasibility study of Cape Cod commuter rail service. Middleborough–Buzzards Bay shuttle service with seven daily round trips was expected to have 1,710 total daily boardings, while Middleborough–[Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") service with ten daily round trips (including two off-peak Boston round trips) was expected to have 2,540 total daily boardings. Service to Hyannis was not evaluated because the Bourne–Hyannis segment would require significant track and signal improvements to be suitable for commuter service.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-114)
